catalog_quote: Stress and vowel length: the last syllable in a word carries the (main) stress. Concomitant with stress is a lengthening of the vowel. In the word list eliciting situation in which an informant pronounces the words with a certain emphasis and free of context, this lengthening can approach the double length of short (unstressed) vowels. This is always the case with monosyllabic words ending in a consonant. Besides phonetically long vowels, sequences of two like vowels also occur, and it is possible that at least some of the long vowels noted have to be interpreted as vowel sequences. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word stress falls on the final syllable, accompanied by lengthening of the stressed vowel (up to double length in isolated citation forms). Voorhoeve 1975:375 restates: 'the last syllable of a word usually carries the main stress', adding that the language may be 'at least marginally tonal'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described ('(main) stress' implies other prominences but none are located).
new_statements.exceptions: None listed in 1971; 1975 hedges with 'usually'. Possible phonemic pitch: some words (ko:d, mu:d, a:r, sir, a:p) show a consistent level rather than falling-rising contour on the final syllable. Some long vowels may be sequences of two like vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based on tape-recorded elicited wordlists (citation forms, 'free of context') from Bawor, Kagas and Saremit; author notes emphasis in the eliciting situation exaggerates final lengthening. Tentative analysis; 'no phonological differences between the two dialects'.
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve writes 'Sawuj' (1971) / 'Sawuy' (1975) = Glottolog Sawi sawi1257 [saw] (alt. names Sawuy, Aejauroh), spoken on the Ajip, Fajit and Kronkel rivers (villages Kamur, Kagas, Saremit, Bawor etc.). His data are wordlists from Bawor (middle-Ajip dialect), Kagas and Saremit/Sanapai (Fajit-Kronkel dialect); he states there are no phonological differences between the two dialects. Not the Arabic 'Šāwi' Bedouin dialects that pollute Glottolog's bibliography for this glottocode. The earlier scan note ('Sawi (PNG)', 'wordlist only') was wrong on both counts: the language is in Indonesian Papua and Voorhoeve 1971 contains a phonology section with a stress statement.
